PAPER: Corpus Pragmatics (2026) 10:7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s41701-025-00211-7 ORIGINAL PAPER Pragmatic Study on Refusals Performed by Israeli NSHs and Egyptian HSL Learners Ahmed Ibrahim1 Received: 12 February 2025 / Accepted: 28 August 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This study investigated the production of refusal strategies by Egyptian Hebrew learners as a second language (HSL). A total of 40 individuals participated in this study: 20 Israeli native Hebrew speakers (IHs) and 20 Egyptian HSL speakers (EHs). Based on Beebe et al. (in: Scarcella, Andersen, Krashen (eds) Develop- ing communicative competence in second language, Newbury House, Cork, 1990) refusal taxonomy, data were collected using a Discourse Completion Task (DCT) that featured five different social situations in Hebrew to investigate the semantic formulas of refusal. The findings revealed diversity in the refusal strategies used by the Egyptian and Israeli groups, depending on which of the five scenarios they encountered. The results demonstrated that Egyptian Hebrew learners succeeded pragmatically in performing refusals. The results also showed that the participants from both groups most frequently utilized indirect refusal strategies, followed by di- rect strategies and adjuncts to refusals. Moreover, the findings indicate no evidence of pragmatic transfer between native and non-native Hebrew speakers. Keywords Pragmatic competence · Refusal strategies · Speech acts · Pragmatic transfer · Hebrew · Egyptians · Israelis Introduction Second language acquisition (SLA) research initially focused on linguistic compe- tence in a target language until Hymes (1972) argued that Chomsky’s model was inadequate. Therefore, he suggested the term communicative competence, which integrates linguistic competence and sociolinguistic aspects. Hymes (1972) origi- nally defined communicative competence as “the ability to use language in various Ahmed Ibrahim A.maghreby@art.asu.edu.eg 1 Department of Hebrew language, Faculty of Arts, Ain Shams University, Cairo, Egypt 1 3 7 Page 2 of 23 A. Ibrahim communicative situations in a manner that is acceptable not only in terms of gram- maticality but also in terms of social appropriateness” (1972, 272). This theoretical shift fundamentally emphasized that language use is governed by sociocultural and contextual conventions (Wolfson, 1989). Consequently, second language learners should be aware of the appropriateness of language use in a given context, as a lack of pragmatic competence can lead to a communication breakdown in the target lan- guage, which is termed pragmatic failure (Thomas, 1983, 93). Interlanguage Pragmatics One of the most significant aspects of investigating pragmatic failure is interlanguage pragmatics (ILP), which examines how L2 learners acquire and deploy linguistic action patterns in their target language (Kasper & Blum-Kulka, 1993). As an inter- disciplinary field bridging SLA and pragmatics, ILP focuses on speech act realization in L2 contexts. Speech acts, such as apologies, requests, and complaints, have received great attention in second language studies over the years because it has been observed that learners face difficulties and challenges in mastering a second language, including a lack of awareness of the L2 socio-pragmatic rules of a target language and the nega- tive pragmatic transfer from their first language (L1) (Ibid.). Pragmatic Transfer Pragmatic transfer refers to the influence of learners’ L1 pragmatic knowledge on their L2 production, comprehension, and pragmatic acquisition (Kasper, 1992, 207). More specifically, this phenomenon involves the transfer of knowledge from the learner’s L1 to the target language (L2) regarding the sociocultural norms that gov- ern language use. Beebe et al. (1990) stated that pragmatic transfer occurs when L1’s sociocultural aspects are applied in L2 production. She Identified two types of pragmatic transfer: positive and negative. Positive pragmatic transfer is the appropriate application of L1 pragmatic knowledge to the target language (L2), whereas negative pragmatic transfer involves the misapplication of L1 sociocultural behaviors in L2 commu- nication (Kasper, 1992, 212–213). As Kasper and Blum-Kulka (1993) explain, it represents “the influence of first language pragmatic competence on IL pragmatic knowledge that differs from the second language target” (1993, 10). Positive transfer thus facilitates communication when the sociocultural behaviors of the L1 and the target language align, while negative transfer may cause communication breakdowns when they diverge (Darwish, 2018, p. 180). Given these potential communication challenges, ILP researchers have particularly focused on negative pragmatic trans- fer. Significant studies in this area include work by Beebe et al. (1990), Félix-Bras- defer (2003), Chang (2009), Abed (2011), Jafari and Sadeghoghlo (2018), Alrefaee and Al-Ghamdi (2019), Al-Juraywi (2021), Qassim et al. (2021), and Chen (2023). Numerous factors influencing negative pragmatic transfer have been identified by ILP researchers, including The degree of difference in the implementation of speech 1 3 Pragmatic Study on Refusals Performed by Israeli NSHs and Egyptian… Page 3 of 23 7 act rules between L1 and L2; the learner’s L2 proficiency level; and the learner’s familiarity with the L2 cultural environment (Chen, 2023, 1113). Refusal Speech Acts Speech acts are utterances produced by a speaker that require responses from the hearer and involve performing certain actions (Searle, 1969). Refusal has become an important speech act studied in the last three decades, having received more attention than other speech acts, such as requests and apologies in second language studies over the years. The main reason for positioning it at the center of discussions on human interaction is that it is “a highly complex speech act” (Houck & Gass, 1996, 49) and is considered to be more complicated than other speech acts because it is not an initial act but a responsive act to others’ requests, invitations, or offers. This reactive nature significantly limits opportunities for pre-production planning and preparation (Houck & Gass, 1999), resulting in considerable variation in performance among L2 learners from different linguistic backgrounds. In addition, refusals are a highly face-threat- ening act (Brown & Levinson, 1987) because the possibility of offending the inter- locutor is inherent in the act itself. If an L2 learner does not respond appropriately, this may result in a loss of face for the speaker. Consequently, advanced pragmatic competence is necessary for successful refusal performance, enabling speakers to navigate the target language’s sociocultural norms, employ appropriate face-saving maneuvers, and maintain a balance between communicative clarity and social appro- priateness (Houck & Gass, 1996, 49). This demonstrates why the refusal production serves as a critical indicator of pragmatic development in L2 acquisition. Refusal is defined as disapproving the interlocutor’s intentions. Chen et al. (1995, 121) stated that it refers to the speaker denying involvement in an action suggested by an interlocutor. According to Searle (1977), refusals belong to the category of commissives because they commit the speaker to not realizing an action in response to invitations, requests, and offers (cited in Félix-Brasdefer, 2006, 2160). Due to the face-threatening nature of refusals, several studies have been conducted in this area, such as Beebe et al. (1990), Chen (1996), Salder and Eröz (2002), Félix-Brasde- fer (2006), Wannaruk (2008), Campillo et al. (2009), Asmalı (2013), Çiftçi (2016), Durham (2019), AlBugami (2019), Shahi (2022), Varisoglu et al. (2023), Al-Sallal (2024), and Huneety et al. (2024), to examine how interlocutors perform a refusal act in interactions and how they can mitigate the offense of the refusal. One of the most significant classifications of refusal speech acts is Beebe et al.’s (1990) taxonomy (see Appendix A). They classified refusal strategies into direct refusal strategies, indirect refusal strategies, and adjuncts to refusals. Direct strate- gies are utterances in which the propositional content and the speaker’s intention are consistent. Therefore, the direct refusal strategy represents a direct declination to the interlocutor’s request. This indicates that the speaker’s intention to refuse is explicitly expressed. In contrast, indirect refusal strategies, which involve refusing others by uttering something other than a direct refusal, are generally face-saving speech acts in which interlocutors express their intentions indirectly. Adjuncts, the third category, are semantic formulas that cannot stand alone to make a refusal and are always used 1 3 7 Page 4 of 23 A. Ibrahim in conjunction with direct or indirect refusal strategies. However, they also play an important role in refusal. (Zhu, 2023, 128–129) Aim of the Study The current study aimed to investigate how HSL students perform refusal speech acts in response to requests, invitations, and suggestions, considering the social vari- ables of the interlocutors. As a result of these findings, both Egyptian instructors and university students may become more pragmatically aware. To equip students with the pragmatic competence they need to succeed in social interactions in the target language and effectively execute refusals, lecturers may integrate speech acts into their language classes. This study sought to address the following research questions: 1. What types of refusal strategies are employed by Egyptian HSL speakers and Israeli Hebrew native speakers in the given situations? 2. How do refusal strategies differ across the two groups (Israelis and Egyptians), and which social factors influence the choice of strategy? 3. Does Arabic as a first language affect HSL learners’ use of refusal strategies and adjuncts to refusals in Hebrew as a second language? Significance of the Study This study on Hebrew refusals is significant for several reasons: 1. The majority of refusal studies in the field of ILP research have focused on other languages, such as English (Al-Issa, 1998; Allami & Naeimi, 2011; Chang, 2009; Chang, 2011; Chen, 2006; Jafari & Sadeghoghlo, 2018; Lin, 2014; Saud, 2019; Zhang, 2022), and Arabic (Nelson et al., 2002; Al-Issa, 2003; Al-Kahtani, 2005; Morkus, 2009; Al-Dawsari, 2013; Darwish, 2018; Al Kayed, et al. 2020; Al Masaeed et al., 2020). However, no studies have been conducted on Hebrew refusals in a second language. Therefore, the researcher conducted this study to examine how Hebrew learners, as second language speakers, can refuse to par- ticipate in activities or actions proposed by their interlocutors. 2. This study would help Hebrew language learners comprehend their speech pat- terns by increasing their knowledge of the refusal strategies employed to main- tain good relationships, thereby enhancing successful communication. 3. The study would provide Hebrew teachers at Egyptian universities and curricu- lum designers with further information regarding the strategies that students pre- fer when refusing something. This would assist them in identifying the negative or challenging aspects of Egyptian HSL learners’ pragmatic behavior and how to overcome these difficulties and challenges in classrooms by raising the pragmatic awareness of speech acts in general, and refusals in particular, by involving these students in interactive activities. 1 3 Pragmatic Study on Refusals Performed by Israeli NSHs and Egyptian… Page 5 of 23 7 Research Method Participants A total of 40 individuals participated in the study: 20 Israeli native speakers of Hebrew (IHs), including 10 females and 10 males, and 20 Egyptian HSL speakers of Hebrew (EHs), also comprising 10 females and 10 males. The age range of all groups was 20–35 years. The participants in the Egyptian group had Hebrew as a major in the Hebrew Language Department, and none of them had traveled to Israel, where Hebrew is utilized as a means of communication. Instrument and Procedures Given the prevalence of discourse completion tests (DCTs) in interlanguage prag- matic studies, this research employed a DCT as its primary data collection instru- ment. As one of the most widely used methods for eliciting production data, a DCT comprises a written questionnaire featuring “brief descriptions of situations” (Houck & Gass, 1996, 46) followed by incomplete dialogues with blank spaces for respon- dents to produce the target refusal speech act (Kasper & Dahl, 1991, 221). The study’s DCT questionnaire included five distinct social contexts for Hebrew refusal scenarios (see Appendix C). To evaluate non-native Hebrew speakers’ pragmatic competence, participants were instructed to read each scenario, imagine themselves in the described situations, and formulate appropriate Hebrew refusal responses. All scenarios reflected authentic university contexts, such as declining to lend a laptop to a classmate or refusing (as a professor) to extend a student’s project deadline. These situations were systematically categorized according to three social vari- ables: social distance, power relationships, and ranking of imposition to test the choice refusal speech act strategies by manipulating these variables. In each situ- ation, a description illustrating the situational context, the participant’s role, and the distance between the interlocutors was provided. By employing an appropriate refusal in the given context, five conversational scenarios for refusal speech acts were designed to assess participants’ pragmatic competence alongside language compe- tency. Through a comparative analysis of Egyptian L2 Hebrew learners and native speakers’ responses, the study evaluated learners’ pragmatic competence in Hebrew refusals, determined the degree to which their refusal strategies approximated native speaker norms, and identified potential pragmatic transfer from Arabic (L1) in the given contexts. Data Analysis The collected participant responses were systematically coded according to Beebe et al.’s (1990) taxonomy of refusal strategies. Each response was analyzed and cat- egorized into one of three primary semantic categories: direct, indirect, or adjunct to refusals. The analysis revealed that responses typically consisted of sequential com- binations of semantic formulas, such as “ani asuk hayom. ani lo yexol lavo axaray ha-tzuhurayim. mah da’atxa nipagesh maxar? I am busy today. I cannot come this 1 3 7 Page 6 of 23 A. Ibrahim afternoon. How about meeting tomorrow?”. The semantic formula consists of three parts: (1) Ani asuk hayom. I am busy today. (statement of regret) (2) Ani lo yaxol lavo axaray haçuhurayim. I cannot come this afternoon. (explana- tion + negative ability) (3) Ma da’atxa nipageš maxar? How about meeting tomorrow? (statement of alternative) Following the coding procedure, the analysis examined participants’ refusal strate- gies in terms of the frequency and choice of semantic formulas. Subsequently, the frequency of refusal strategies of the two groups (Egyptian HSLs and Israeli HNSs) was compared by calculating the total number of each semantic formula used by each group in all five situational contexts, as shown in the tables. The tables facilitated the researcher in comparing the overall frequency of use of each semantic formula. The first study question demonstrated the strategies employed by both groups and individuals of varied statuses. The study highlighted similarities and differences in the most commonly used Hebrew refusal strategies, while considering the standing of the interlocutors after the general comparisons. Consequently, this study provided a thorough response to the second research question. Moreover, responses from both genders in each group were examined and compared. Finally, the responses of Egyp- tian Hebrew learners to the third research question were investigated to determine whether or not there were any effects of their L1 on the target language. Inter-Rater Reliability Two qualified raters independently coded a randomly selected 50% of the total data (100 responses from 40 participants, with 20 responses per scenario). Cohen’s Kappa (κ), which accounts for chance agreement, was assessed using inter-rater agreement (Cohen, 1960). The analysis revealed almost perfect agreement: κ = 0.81 (95% CI [0.67, 0.95]) (Landis & Koch, 1977) (see Appendix B). This high reliability supports frequency comparisons between the Israeli and Egyptian groups. Results The data analysis results provided answers to each of the research questions. What Types of Refusal Strategies are Employed by Egyptian HSL Speakers and Israeli Native Speakers in Hebrew? The results showed that the total number of refusal strategies employed by Israelis was 294, while that employed by Egyptians was 317. Figure 1 illustrates the fre- quency number of refusal categories, which are divided into three categories: direct, indirect, and adjuncts. 1 3 Pragmatic Study on Refusals Performed by Israeli NSHs and Egyptian… Page 7 of 23 7 Fig. 1 Frequency number of refusal categories by IHs and EHs Figure 1 shows that Israeli native speakers employed indirect strategies most fre- quently, with a total of 176 times (60%), followed by direct strategies at 66 times (22%), while adjunct strategies were used the least at 52 times (18%). Conversely, Egyptian HSL students demonstrated similar trends; they employed indirect strat- egies most frequently, with 217 occurrences (68%), followed by direct strategies 56 occurrences (18%), and the least used were adjunct strategies at 44 occurrences (14%). This indicates that Egyptian Hebrew learners effectively realized refusals in context and reduced the degree of offense by utilizing various indirect refusal strate- gies, such as explanations, apologies, and alternatives. Notably, the Egyptian group employed indirect refusals (217 times) more than the Israeli group (176 times); how- ever, the Israeli participants used direct strategies (66 times) and adjuncts (52 times) more than the Egyptian participants (56 and 44 times, respectively). How do Refusal Strategies Differ Across the Two Groups (Israelis and Egyptians) in Hebrew, and Which Social Factors May Influence the Choice of Strategy? The results of the data analysis in Table 1 revealed that the Egyptian participants employed most of the refusal strategies used by Israelis; however, there was a differ- ence between the two groups regarding the frequency of refusal strategy realization. In terms of direct refusal strategies, the most preferred sub-strategy for both groups was non-performatives (61 times by Israelis and 56 times by Egyptians). However, the performative sub-strategy was used only by Israelis (five times) in most situa- tions. Egyptians may not have used performative refusals for two reasons: first, they perceived the situations as having a higher degree of imposition than Israelis did; second, they did not want to be considered rude and aimed to preserve their inter- locutor’s face. With respect to the social factor of gender, the results in Table 2 show that there is no significant difference between males and females in each group (Israelis and Egyptians) in the frequency of refusal realization. A chi-square test confirmed this finding, indicating that the difference between the two genders in both groups was not significant at p < 0.05 in all five situations. For example, in Situa- tion 2, the chi-square test indicated that there was no significant difference between Israeli males and females in performing refusals (the p value was 0.4386, which is >0.05). Additionally, the results of the chi-square test showed that Egyptian males used refusals similarly to Egyptian females in situation 2 (p value= 0.1760, which is >0.05). Unexpectedly, power and social distance did not significantly influence the refusal strategy choice. The results showed a trend toward indirect refusal strategies in all situations, regardless of hearer power. For instance, in situations 3 (where the speaker has no power over the hearer) and 4 (where there is no power difference between the interlocutors), indirect refusals were the preferred strategy for both Israeli and Egyp- tian groups. Furthermore, in Situation 2, although the professor (speaker) has power over the student (hearer), indirect refusals were the most frequently used strategy by both groups. As seen in Table 2, there were various semantic formulas were used by Israelis and Egyptians to express non-performative refusal acts, which were divided into four types accord- ing to the responses of the two groups: negation (e.g., lo no), inability (e.g., lo oxal I cannot) (iy ifšar it is not possible), unwillingness (e.g., ani lo roça I do not want), and disapproval (e.g., ani lo me’ašer lexa I do not approve of you), (ani lo maskim I do not agree). The results in Figure 2 show a similarity between both groups in the frequency of employing non-performative refusal sub-strategies (61 times by Israelis and 56 times by Egyptians). Negative ability was the most frequently used sub-strategy for non-performative refusals by Israelis and Egyptians (64% and 68%, respectively). In contrast, negation was the least employed sub-strategy in non-performative refusals, used by Israelis 5% of the time and by Egyptians, 9%. In terms of indirect refusals, explanation was the most frequently utilized strat- egy by both groups, containing content that could be compared more thoroughly. Explanations can be divided into two categories: unspecific and specific excuses. Unspecific excuses included one type, which is general excuses, such as “ani asuk I am busy”, “yeš li kvar toxniyot axarot ha’arev I already have other plans for this evening”, “kavati mašehu axer be’oto erev I scheduled something else that evening”. Specific excuses were classified into five types: needs, such as “ki ani çarix oto lali- modim because I need it for study”; time, such as “ani mištameš bo karega’ I am using it right now”; “ki hozmanti laxatuna be’oto yum because I was invited to a wedding that day”; personal, such as “hamaxšev šeli me’od yakar vani ma’adif lo latet oto la’axarim my laptop is very expensive and I prefer not to lend it to others”; feelings, such as “ani mergiš lo benuax leheçtaref lemexlaka axeret I feel uncomfortable join- ing another department”; “hanoseh šehiça’ta li lo mamaš lo moçe xen be’enay I don’t really like the topic you suggested”; and issues, such as “as “hamaxšev šeli me’od yašan ve-me’od itti my laptop is quite old and very slow”, “nišaru lei axozim bodedim besulela, ki hamaxšev šeli alul lehaxbot be’emça haprezençya I have a few percent left in the battery, because my laptop may turn off in the middle of the presentation”. As can be seen in Figure 3, there is a similarity between Israeli and Egyptian par- ticipants in the frequency of employing sub-strategies of explanation (78 times by Israelis and 82 times by Egyptians). Both groups tended to use specific explanations more than unspecific explanations. Personal reasons were the most used sub-strategy in explanations by the two groups to express excuses for refusals (40% and 36%, respectively). For instance, the Israeli group used personal excuses, such as “yeš li gam avodat seminar še-alay lehagiš I also have a seminar to submit.” On the other hand, the Egyptian group utilized similar personal excuses to Israelis, such as “ki ani gam yeš li mivxan because I also have a test.” The sub-strategy of issues was the least used sub-strategy in the explanation strategy, employed by Israelis 8% and Egyp- tians 2%. This indicates that there is no evidence of pragmatic transfer from L1 to L2 in Egyptian Hebrew learners’ realiza- tion of refusals, neither in the frequency nor in the content of the semantic formulas. 1 3 Pragmatic Study on Refusals Performed by Israeli NSHs and Egyptian… Page 13 of 23 7 Discussion The study’s findings presented that there was no difference between Egyptian and Israeli participants in refusing a request, suggestion, or invitation. Both groups preferred to utilize indirect strategies to minimize the degree of face-threatening refusals. Chen (1996) stated that indirect strategies, which require a high pragmatic competence level, are frequently employed to realize refusals. In interactions, it is more complicated to perform a refusal because it may necessitate extensive nego- tiating maneuvers to avoid threatening the interlocutor’s face, which can lead to a breakdown in communication (Campillo et al., 2009, 140). Therefore, the partici- pants tended to integrate two or more indirect sub-strategies, such as “ani me’od meçta’eret, aval hamaxšev šeli me’od yakar I am very sorry, but my laptop is very expensive” (statement of regret + excuse) and “ani meçta’er axi, aval yeš li gam avo- dat seminar še-alay lehagiš. laxuti yeš maxšev, oxal livdok bešvilxa. I am sorry bro, but I also have a seminar to submit. My sister has a laptop. I can check it for you.” (statement of regret + excuse + alternative), to mitigate the degree of refusal because they were aware of the face-threatening nature of refusals. Furthermore, to avoid offending the interlocutor, Egyptian Hebrew learners who performed a refusal directly used only non-performative expressions, such as “lo karega’ not now”, “ani lo yexola I cannot”, “en maçav leha’arix et hamu’ed še-kava’nu meroš there is no chance to extend the date that we have set in advance”, and “ze lo efšzri axšav it is not possible right now.” In contrast, Israeli participants employed not only non-performatives but also performative refusals, such as “ani asarev I refuse” and “eçtarex lesarev lehazmana I have to refuse the invitation.” While Brown and Levinson’s (1987) politeness theory posits that such direct performatives inher- ently threaten an interlocutor’s negative face, the study’s results revealed that native Hebrew speakers systematically mitigated this face threat with supportive moves. For example, they included address terms and expressions of appreciation alongside direct performatives, such as “ani modah lexa me’od al hahaçta’a, avel ani asarev I thank you very much for the suggestion, but I must refuse”, and “profesor yakar, toda raba al hahaçta’a, avel ani ne’leçet lesarev Dear Professor, thank you very much for the suggestion, but I have to refuse”; “leça’ari, eçtarex lesarev lehazmana unfor- tunately, I have to refuse the invitation”. Perhaps the Egyptian participants did not prefer to use performative refusals because they perceived the situations as more imposing than the Israeli participants did and wanted to preserve their interlocutor’s face. Moreover, Egyptians employed adjuncts to refusals the least frequently. The most frequently used sub-strategies of adjuncts were statements of positive opinion, such as “hayiti me’od sameyax lavo ax... I would be very happy to come, but…”, “nišma me’od meanyen, aval... it sounds very interesting, but…”, “hanose meanyen aval... the topic is interesting, but…”; and statements of appreciation, such as “toda raba al hahazmana thanks a lot for the invitation”, “toda al hahaçta’a thanks for the sugges- tion.” Notably, the two groups tended to employ adjuncts, which are not considered an independent strategy, as a means of mitigating the effect of the refusal act on their interlocutor. In general, the findings presented that the invitation situation received the highest rating. This indicates that when participants are invited, they make more 1 3 7 Page 14 of 23 A. Ibrahim effort to decline politely. However, the suggestion situations received the lowest score, followed by the request situations. This implies that participants exerted less effort to refuse suggestions. Finally, the findings revealed that social status did not significantly influence refusal strategy choice in relation to refusal situation type. Native and non-native Hebrew speakers used indirect strategies more than other strategies in all situations, irrespective of the hearer’s power, distance, or gender. This implies that the interac- tion between Israelis and Egyptians in performing refusals does not lead to a com- munication breakdown. Conclusion This study examined the use of refusal strategies by Egyptian HSL speakers com- pared to Israeli native speakers of Hebrew. The study’s findings showed that both Israeli native Hebrew speakers and Egyptian HSL learners utilized a wide range of refusal strategies (N = 663 in total). Both groups preferred indirect strategies over direct refusals strategies in all five contexts. This finding is consistent with Chen’s (1996) and Nelson et al. (2002) findings. Statements of regret, explanations, and alternative strategies were the most frequent semantic formulas for refusal strategies in this study. Explanation was the most frequently utilized sub-strategy employed by Egyptian and Israeli participants to indirectly realize refusals. This result aligns with Al-Issa (2003) and Nelson et al. (2002). Furthermore, the findings presented that there was no significant difference between the males and females in each group in realizing refusals, which implies that the social variable of gender was not influ- enced by strategy choice. This result is in line with Blum-Kulka et al. (1985) findings and inconsistent with Lakoff (1973) hypothesis that women are less direct than men. Moreover, the other two social variables (power and social distance) were not related to the refusal strategy choice. This result is not consistent with Félix-Brasdefer’s (2006) finding that both social dimensions are significantly related to strategy type choice. Finally, Egyptian HSL learners tended to give similar excuses when refusing as native Hebrew speakers did, which indicates that there is no significant pragmatic transfer between the two groups in the content of the explanation strategy. This result is not consistent with those of Beebe et al. (1990) and Kwon (2003). This indicates that the Egyptian HSL participants were pragmatically competent; they were aware of the face-threatening potential of the interlocutor while refusing and how to refuse appropriately. Limitations of the Study In this study, there are certain limitations that should be emphasized, as they could influence the findings’ generalizability to other situations. Initially, the analysis focused only on the speaker’s expressions of rejection. Reactions to refusals fall out- side the scope of this research; however, they are a vital topic for further exploration. Second, employing the DCT approach to capture refusals as speech acts revealed a methodological constraint. The DCT was implemented with the belief that the data 1 3 Pragmatic Study on Refusals Performed by Israeli NSHs and Egyptian… Page 15 of 23 7 gathered would closely resemble naturally occurring data and that the DCT serves as an effective and efficient method for data collection because of its benefits, including the capacity to generate substantial amounts of comparable and diverse data on refusal speech acts. The limitation of this approach lies in its failure to efficiently gather the dynamic aspects of discourse found in daily situations, such as pragmatic elements, turn-taking, and conversation structure (Barron, 2003). Consequently, even with the benefits of the process, DCTs might “conceal the sequential and jointly constructed character of conversation” (Turnbull, 2001, 35). Third, the sample of participants in this study presents another limitation. The sample does not fully reflect Hebrew- language learners at various universities in Egypt. All the Egyptian participants were from one university; therefore, the findings of this study may not be generalizable to Egyptian HSL students at other universities in Egypt. Additionally, the number of participants was limited for two reasons: first, a limited number of students learning Hebrew in Egypt; second, the study was halted in Israeli universities because of the ongoing war, which makes it difficult to communicate with Israelis and encourage them to participate. Fourth, this study focused exclusively on verbal expressions of refusal. Although natural communication among speakers depends on both verbal and nonverbal actions (such as facial expressions, gestures, and tone of voice), which are vital for interpreting speech acts (Searle, 1975), the study did not cover the latter. Pedagogical Implications for Developing Pragmatic Awareness of L2 Hebrew Refusal Strategies The findings of the study reveal how important it is to conduct practical awareness- raising activities to help L2 learners effectively develop refusal strategies. Instruc- tors should provide L2 learners with contrastive analysis tasks that compare refusal norms in their L1 (Arabic) and L2 (Hebrew) to achieve the best learning outcomes. These tasks should examine how different cultures use indirect refusal strategies (e.g., explanations, alternative suggestions) to mitigate face threats. Learners can enhance their metapragmatic awareness of what is contextually appropriate (e.g., power, imposition) through guided activities, such as analyzing refusal sequences or critically evaluating their own Discourse Completion Task (DCT) responses. Addi- tionally, interactive role-plays with immediate feedback that focus on verbal and non- verbal cues (tone, gestures) could bridge the gap between controlled DCT responses and real interactional competence. These types of activities would help learners pre- pare for sociopragmatic variation by exposing them to it in a structured way. JSON: Name: hebrew_refusal_transfer_pipeline Title: Multimodal comparative analysis using discourse completion tasks and role-plays to evaluate pragmatic transfer in Hebrew refusal strategies of Egyptian HSL learners versus Israeli native speakers Short Hypothesis: If Egyptian HSL learners transfer Arabic L1 pragmatic norms into Hebrew, then, after controlling for proficiency and situational variables, Egyptian participants will produce a significantly different distribution of refusal semantic formulas than Israeli native Hebrew speakers. Related Work: Interlanguage pragmatics research has extensively used discourse completion tasks (DCTs) and taxonomies (e.g., direct/indirect/adjunct categories) to compare L1–L2 pragmatic behavior across languages; many studies report pragmatic transfer effects, proficiency dependence, and sensitivity to social variables (power, distance, imposition). Prior work is concentrated on English and Arabic, generally uses DCTs or questionnaires, often employs small convenience samples, and relies on written or audio-only elicitation. Limitations in existing approaches include: heavy reliance on DCTs that lack interactional sequencing and multimodal cues; inconsistent control for L2 proficiency and exposure; limited sample sizes and single-institution sampling; inconsistent statistical modeling of item and subject variance; and scarce studies on Hebrew as L2. These weaknesses leave unresolved whether observed differences reflect genuine pragmatic transfer, data-collection artifacts, or effects of proficiency, modality, and situational embedding. Abstract: This research pipeline defines a multimodal empirical protocol to test pragmatic transfer hypotheses in Hebrew refusal production by Egyptian learners (HSL) relative to Israeli native speakers. The pipeline combines written discourse completion tasks, audio–video role-play interactions, and a small naturalistic classroom corpus to capture both planned and interactional refusals. Responses are annotated with a fine-grained refusal taxonomy (direct/indirect/adjunct subtypes) and coded for social variables (power, distance, imposition), proficiency, and exposure. Statistical models (mixed-effects logistic regression) will quantify group differences while controlling for participant and item variance, and automated classifiers will be developed to reproduce human annotations for scalability. The main contribution is a reproducible, multimodal experimental design that isolates modality and proficiency effects from genuine pragmatic transfer, producing effect-size estimates and annotation resources that clarify whether and how Arabic L1 influences Hebrew refusal forms. Expected outcomes include robust statistical tests of transfer, an annotated multimodal refusal corpus in Hebrew, and evaluative benchmarks for future ILP studies. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Elicited DCT dataset: 200 participants (100 Egyptian HSL learners stratified by low/medium/high Hebrew proficiency; 100 Israeli native speakers), each answering 10 refusal scenarios varying power (high/low), social distance (close/distant), and imposition (low/medium/high). (2) Role-play dataset: subset of 80 participants (40 EH, 40 IH) performing 6 scripted role-play interactions per participant, audio+video recorded. (3) Naturalistic corpus: ~50 short classroom/meeting interactions (recorded, consented) containing refusals. Baselines: (A) original DCT-only analysis pipeline (Beebe taxonomy, frequency counts, chi-square); (B) written-only vs multimodal comparison; (C) human-annotated gold standard for classification. Annotation: two trained raters annotate all items for semantic formula, adjuncts, and social variables; compute Cohen's kappa. Statistical evaluation: primary outcome = distribution difference in refusal semantic formulas between EH and IH. Models: mixed-effects logistic regression with random intercepts for participant and item; fixed effects = group, proficiency, social variables, modality, and their interactions. Report p-values, odds ratios, 95% CIs, and Cohen's d for effect sizes. Secondary analyses: (1) mixed-effects models predicting use of specific sub-strategies (explanation, statement of regret, alternative); (2) mediation analysis testing proficiency as mediator of group effect. Automated classification: train a multi-class classifier (text+audio prosody+visual head/gesture features) to predict refusal subtype; evaluation via stratified 10-fold cross-validation; metrics = accuracy, macro F1, precision, recall. Ablation studies: (i) DCT-only vs role-play-only vs combined datasets to measure modality effect; (ii) classifier ablation removing prosody and visual features to quantify multimodal contribution; (iii) model ablation removing proficiency covariate to assess confounding. Power calculation: N=200 yields >0.80 power to detect small-to-medium group odds ratio ~1.6 at alpha=0.05 given estimated item ICCs. Reporting: confusion matrices, effect-size tables, and full model coefficients. Risk Factors and Limitations: Ecological validity: DCT responses may not reflect interactional behavior; role-plays may still be partly scripted. Sampling bias: participants from limited institutions or self-selection may reduce generalizability. Annotation subjectivity: taxonomy boundary cases and adjunct coding can produce rater disagreement; inter-rater reliability may be below acceptable thresholds. Confounding variables: unmeasured exposure to Israeli media, bilingualism, or regional dialects may confound group effects. Small effect sizes: pragmatic transfer effects may be subtle and require larger samples than planned. Political/logistical constraints: access to Israeli participants or cross-border data collection may be restricted, limiting balanced sampling. Multimodal processing limits: automatic extraction of robust visual and prosodic features requires high-quality recordings and compute resources; noise or low-resolution video will reduce classifier performance. Ethical risks: sensitive content and identifiable video data require strict consent and secure storage protocols, which may limit data sharing. Language transcription errors: Hebrew/Arabic orthographic and transliteration inconsistencies may bias automated text features.
